lobby.title: Museum of Indian History
lobby.welcome: Welcome to the Museum of Indian History. Six galleries around this court tell the story of India, from the first stone tools to the Republic. Choose a gallery from the doorways around you, or start with Ancient India on your left. At any object, tap or gaze to hear its audio guide.

wings.title: Ancient India
wings.subtitle: From the first toolmakers to the early kingdoms
wings.intro: Some of the oldest stone tools in South Asia, about 1.5 million years old, come from Attirampakkam near Chennai. Over hundreds of thousands of years people here became farmers and then city-builders: by 2600 BCE the Indus Civilisation had planned cities with drains, standard weights and a script that is still undeciphered. After its decline came the age of the Vedas and, by the sixth century BCE, kingdoms, coins and new religions.

items.title: Rock paintings of Bhimbetka
items.where: In situ, Bhimbetka rock shelters, Madhya Pradesh (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
items.label: More than 750 rock shelters in the Vindhya hills hold paintings of hunters, dancers, horses, elephants and wild cattle, made with red and white mineral pigments. The oldest layers are thought to date from the Mesolithic period, making them among the earliest known art in India.
items.narration: Rock paintings of Bhimbetka. More than 750 rock shelters in the Vindhya hills hold paintings of hunters, dancers, horses, elephants and wild cattle, made with red and white mineral pigments. The oldest layers are thought to date from the Mesolithic period, making them among the earliest known art in India. The shelters were recognised by the archaeologist V. S. Wakankar in 1957, who noticed the rock formations from a train. Some shelters were used for many thousands of years, so later paintings often cover earlier ones.

items.title: The 'Priest-King'
items.label: Found at Mohenjo-daro in the mid-1920s, this bearded man wears a band around his head and a robe decorated with trefoil patterns that were once filled with red paste. Archaeologists nicknamed him the 'Priest-King', but nobody knows who he really was – the Indus script has never been deciphered.
items.narration: The 'Priest-King'. Found at Mohenjo-daro in the mid-1920s, this bearded man wears a band around his head and a robe decorated with trefoil patterns that were once filled with red paste. Archaeologists nicknamed him the 'Priest-King', but nobody knows who he really was – the Indus script has never been deciphered. Mohenjo-daro was one of the largest cities of the Bronze Age world, with tens of thousands of people living in streets laid out on a grid, with covered drains and brick houses. Yet it has no grand palaces or royal tombs, which is one reason its rulers remain a mystery.

items.title: The 'Dancing Girl'
items.label: Only 10.5 centimetres tall, this young woman stands with one hand on her hip and her left arm covered in bangles. She was found at Mohenjo-daro in 1926 and is one of the finest metal sculptures of the Indus Civilisation, cast about four thousand years ago.
items.narration: The 'Dancing Girl'. Only 10.5 centimetres tall, this young woman stands with one hand on her hip and her left arm covered in bangles. She was found at Mohenjo-daro in 1926 and is one of the finest metal sculptures of the Indus Civilisation, cast about four thousand years ago. Lost-wax casting means the figure was first modelled in wax, covered in clay and heated so that the wax ran out, leaving a mould for molten metal. Bangles like hers are still worn across South Asia today.

items.title: The 'Pashupati' seal
items.label: Indus seals were pressed into clay to mark goods. This one shows a horned figure seated cross-legged, surrounded by an elephant, a tiger, a rhinoceros and a buffalo. Early scholars linked the figure to the god Shiva as 'lord of animals', but its meaning is still debated.
items.narration: The 'Pashupati' seal. Indus seals were pressed into clay to mark goods. This one shows a horned figure seated cross-legged, surrounded by an elephant, a tiger, a rhinoceros and a buffalo. Early scholars linked the figure to the god Shiva as 'lord of animals', but its meaning is still debated. Hundreds of Indus seals have been found, many carrying a short inscription above an animal. Some reached Mesopotamia, showing that Indus merchants traded across the Arabian Sea more than four thousand years ago.

items.title: The Great Bath, Mohenjo-daro
items.medium: Fired brick, gypsum mortar and bitumen; about 12 × 7 m, 2.4 m deep
items.where: In situ, Mohenjo-daro, Sindh (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
items.label: On Mohenjo-daro's raised citadel lies a watertight brick tank with steps at both ends. Its bricks were set in gypsum mortar and sealed with a layer of bitumen. It may have been used for ritual bathing – an early sign of the importance of water and purity in South Asian religion.
items.narration: The Great Bath, Mohenjo-daro. On Mohenjo-daro's raised citadel lies a watertight brick tank with steps at both ends. Its bricks were set in gypsum mortar and sealed with a layer of bitumen. It may have been used for ritual bathing – an early sign of the importance of water and purity in South Asian religion. The bath was surrounded by a colonnade and small rooms, and a large drain carried its water away. Careful planning like this, repeated across hundreds of Indus towns, is what makes the civilisation so remarkable.

items.title: A manuscript of the Rigveda
items.date: Hymns composed c. 1500–1200 BCE; manuscript 19th century
items.label: The Rigveda is a collection of 1,028 hymns in Vedic Sanskrit, composed in north-western India and passed down by word of mouth with remarkable precision for many centuries before being written down. Manuscripts like this are much later copies.
items.narration: A manuscript of the Rigveda. The Rigveda is a collection of 1,028 hymns in Vedic Sanskrit, composed in north-western India and passed down by word of mouth with remarkable precision for many centuries before being written down. Manuscripts like this are much later copies. Priests memorised the hymns with elaborate recitation methods, chanting the words in different orders so that not a syllable would change. In 2007 a collection of Rigveda manuscripts kept in Pune was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.

items.title: Punch-marked coins
items.label: India's earliest coins were small pieces of silver stamped with symbols such as the sun, animals, trees and hills, one punch at a time. They circulated in the Mahajanapadas – 'great realms' such as Magadha, Kosala and Avanti – as trade and cities grew in the Ganga plain.
items.narration: Punch-marked coins. India's earliest coins were small pieces of silver stamped with symbols such as the sun, animals, trees and hills, one punch at a time. They circulated in the Mahajanapadas – 'great realms' such as Magadha, Kosala and Avanti – as trade and cities grew in the Ganga plain. Magadha, with its capital at Pataliputra, gradually defeated its rivals and became the heart of India's first great empire, the Mauryan Empire.

centre.title: Painted storage jar (replica)
centre.medium: Replica of wheel-thrown red ware painted in black
centre.label: Harappan potters threw large jars on the wheel, coated them with a red slip and painted them in black with bands, intersecting circles and leaf patterns. Jars like this stored grain, oil and water in Indus houses. This replica is based on vessels excavated at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro.
centre.narration: Painted storage jar (replica). Harappan potters threw large jars on the wheel, coated them with a red slip and painted them in black with bands, intersecting circles and leaf patterns. Jars like this stored grain, oil and water in Indus houses. This replica is based on vessels excavated at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro. Pottery is the most common find at Indus sites. Because styles changed over time, archaeologists use broken pieces of pots, called sherds, to date the layers in which they are found.

quiz.q: Which UNESCO World Heritage Site in Madhya Pradesh is famous for its prehistoric rock paintings?
quiz.why: Bhimbetka's rock shelters hold thousands of paintings, the earliest probably Mesolithic.

quiz.q: Which Harappan site, in the Rann of Kutch, had rock-cut reservoirs and a large signboard of Indus signs?
quiz.why: Dholavira on Khadir island had remarkable reservoirs and a ten-sign signboard near a gateway.

quiz.q: How many hymns does the Rigveda contain?
quiz.why: The Rigveda has 1,028 hymns arranged in ten mandalas.

quiz.q: Where did the Buddha give his first sermon?
quiz.why: He attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya and gave his first sermon at Sarnath.

quiz.q: How many great states, or mahajanapadas, do Buddhist and Jain texts list?
quiz.why: The texts list sixteen mahajanapadas around the 6th century BCE.

quiz.q: Which Persian king conquered Gandhara and the Indus region in the late 6th century BCE?
quiz.why: Darius I made the region a tribute-paying province of the Achaemenid empire.

wings.title: Classical India
wings.subtitle: The age of empires
wings.intro: In 321 BCE Chandragupta Maurya founded an empire that, under his grandson Ashoka, covered most of the subcontinent. Later dynasties – the Shungas, Satavahanas, Kushans and Guptas – presided over flourishing trade, Buddhist and Hindu art, and advances in mathematics, astronomy and literature. In the far south, the Sangam poems of the Tamil country describe the kingdoms of the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas.

items.title: Lion Capital of Ashoka
items.label: Four lions stand back to back on a drum carved with a horse, a bull, an elephant and a lion separated by wheels, above an inverted lotus. The capital crowned a pillar Ashoka set up where the Buddha gave his first sermon. Adopted as India's national emblem in 1950, its wheel also appears on the national flag.
items.narration: Lion Capital of Ashoka. Four lions stand back to back on a drum carved with a horse, a bull, an elephant and a lion separated by wheels, above an inverted lotus. The capital crowned a pillar Ashoka set up where the Buddha gave his first sermon. Adopted as India's national emblem in 1950, its wheel also appears on the national flag. Ashoka turned to Buddhism after his bloody conquest of Kalinga, and spread messages of dhamma – moral conduct and tolerance – through edicts carved on rocks and pillars across his empire.
items.query: Lion Capital of Ashoka Sarnath museum

items.title: Didarganj Yakshi
items.medium: Polished Chunar sandstone, about 1.6 m high
items.label: This life-size female attendant holding a fly-whisk was found on the bank of the Ganga at Didarganj, Patna, in 1917. Its mirror-like polish is typical of Mauryan stone carving, though some scholars date it later. Yakshis were nature spirits associated with fertility and abundance.
items.narration: Didarganj Yakshi. This life-size female attendant holding a fly-whisk was found on the bank of the Ganga at Didarganj, Patna, in 1917. Its mirror-like polish is typical of Mauryan stone carving, though some scholars date it later. Yakshis were nature spirits associated with fertility and abundance. Patna stands on the site of Pataliputra, the Mauryan capital, which the Greek ambassador Megasthenes described as a vast city protected by a timber wall.

items.title: The Great Stupa at Sanchi
items.medium: Brick core cased in stone; carved sandstone gateways
items.where: In situ, Sanchi, Madhya Pradesh (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
items.label: Ashoka built the first brick stupa here to enshrine relics of the Buddha. It was later enlarged and cased in stone, and four magnificent gateways (toranas) were added, carved with stories from the Buddha's past and present lives.
items.narration: The Great Stupa at Sanchi. Ashoka built the first brick stupa here to enshrine relics of the Buddha. It was later enlarged and cased in stone, and four magnificent gateways (toranas) were added, carved with stories from the Buddha's past and present lives. A stupa is a solid dome that pilgrims walk around clockwise in devotion. Many of the carvings at Sanchi were paid for by ordinary donors – ivory carvers, merchants, monks and nuns – whose names are inscribed in the stone.

items.title: Standing Buddha from Gandhara
items.label: Under the Kushan emperors, sculptors in Gandhara – today's north-western Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan – created some of the earliest images of the Buddha in human form. Wavy hair, deeply folded robes and calm faces show the influence of Greek and Roman art blended with Indian ideas.
items.narration: Standing Buddha from Gandhara. Under the Kushan emperors, sculptors in Gandhara – today's north-western Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan – created some of the earliest images of the Buddha in human form. Wavy hair, deeply folded robes and calm faces show the influence of Greek and Roman art blended with Indian ideas. At the same time, sculptors at Mathura in northern India were making Buddha images in red sandstone in a purely Indian style. The Kushan king Kanishka ruled over both regions and was a great patron of Buddhism.

items.title: Gold coin of Samudragupta
items.label: The Gupta kings issued fine gold coins called dinaras. On this type Samudragupta is shown seated, playing a veena – a reminder that he was praised as a poet and musician as well as a conqueror. The Gupta period is often called a classical age of Indian art and learning.
items.narration: Gold coin of Samudragupta. The Gupta kings issued fine gold coins called dinaras. On this type Samudragupta is shown seated, playing a veena – a reminder that he was praised as a poet and musician as well as a conqueror. The Gupta period is often called a classical age of Indian art and learning. His achievements are recorded in a long Sanskrit poem carved on the Allahabad pillar, the same pillar that already carried an inscription of Ashoka six hundred years earlier.

items.title: Padmapani, Ajanta Cave 1
items.where: In situ, Ajanta Caves, Maharashtra (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
items.label: About thirty Buddhist caves were cut into a horseshoe-shaped cliff at Ajanta between the 2nd century BCE and the late 5th century CE. This bodhisattva of compassion, holding a lotus, is one of the most celebrated wall paintings of Cave 1.
items.narration: Padmapani, Ajanta Cave 1. About thirty Buddhist caves were cut into a horseshoe-shaped cliff at Ajanta between the 2nd century BCE and the late 5th century CE. This bodhisattva of compassion, holding a lotus, is one of the most celebrated wall paintings of Cave 1. The caves were abandoned and forgotten for centuries until a British officer, John Smith, stumbled on them while hunting a tiger in 1819.

items.title: The Shore Temple, Mamallapuram
items.where: In situ, Mamallapuram, Tamil Nadu (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
items.label: Built under the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II, the Shore Temple is one of the earliest structural stone temples in South India. Its stepped towers anticipate the great temples of the Cholas. It stands beside the Bay of Bengal.
items.narration: The Shore Temple, Mamallapuram. Built under the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II, the Shore Temple is one of the earliest structural stone temples in South India. Its stepped towers anticipate the great temples of the Cholas. It stands beside the Bay of Bengal. Mamallapuram was a busy Pallava port. Nearby, artists carved a huge rock face with the scene known as Arjuna's Penance or the Descent of the Ganges, one of the largest open-air reliefs in the world.

centre.title: The Iron Pillar of Delhi (replica)
centre.medium: Replica of a wrought-iron column, 7.2 m high
centre.label: This towering column was forged from wrought iron about 1,600 years ago and weighs some six tonnes. A Sanskrit inscription honours a king named Chandra, usually identified as the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II. Now in the Qutb complex in Delhi, the pillar has barely rusted, thanks to a thin protective film rich in phosphorus.
centre.narration: The Iron Pillar of Delhi (replica). This towering column was forged from wrought iron about 1,600 years ago and weighs some six tonnes. A Sanskrit inscription honours a king named Chandra, usually identified as the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II. Now in the Qutb complex in Delhi, the pillar has barely rusted, thanks to a thin protective film rich in phosphorus. Forging a single iron object this large was an extraordinary achievement for its time. Metallurgists still study the pillar to understand how its rust-resistant surface formed.

quiz.q: Whom did Chandragupta Maurya overthrow to found the Maurya empire?
quiz.why: He overthrew the Nanda king around 321 BCE.

quiz.q: Which treatise on statecraft is attributed to Chanakya?
quiz.why: The Arthashastra, on statecraft, economy and law, is attributed to Chanakya (Kautilya).

quiz.q: Which Kushana ruler convened the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir?
quiz.why: Kanishka patronised Buddhism and convened the Fourth Buddhist Council.

quiz.q: In Sangam poetry, poems of love are called what?
quiz.why: Akam poems deal with love; puram with war and public life.

quiz.q: At which site near Puducherry have Roman pottery and wine jars been excavated?
quiz.why: Excavations at Arikamedu revealed Roman pottery and amphorae.

quiz.q: Which Chinese pilgrim visited India in the reign of Chandragupta II?
quiz.why: Faxian visited India during Chandragupta II's reign.

wings.title: Medieval India
wings.subtitle: Kingdoms, temples and empires
wings.intro: Between the 8th and 18th centuries India was shaped by powerful regional kingdoms such as the Rashtrakutas, Cholas and Rajputs, by the Delhi Sultanate from 1206, by the Vijayanagara empire in the south and by the Mughals from 1526. Temples, mosques, tombs and forts of this age – and the devotional poetry of Bhakti and Sufi saints – remain among India's greatest cultural treasures.

items.title: Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur
items.where: In situ, Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
items.label: Raja Raja I, the great Chola emperor, built this temple to Shiva at his capital Thanjavur. Its tower rises about 66 metres and is crowned by a huge granite capstone. Inscriptions on its walls list the gifts, dancers, musicians and staff that served the temple.
items.narration: Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur. Raja Raja I, the great Chola emperor, built this temple to Shiva at his capital Thanjavur. Its tower rises about 66 metres and is crowned by a huge granite capstone. Inscriptions on its walls list the gifts, dancers, musicians and staff that served the temple. The Cholas were also a sea power: Raja Raja's son Rajendra sent a naval expedition to South-East Asia, and Chola merchants traded as far as China.

items.title: Shiva Nataraja, Lord of the Dance
items.label: Shiva performs the cosmic dance that destroys and recreates the universe, framed by a ring of fire and trampling the dwarf of ignorance. Chola bronzes like this were carried in temple processions, dressed in silk and jewels. They are among the masterpieces of world metal sculpture.
items.narration: Shiva Nataraja, Lord of the Dance. Shiva performs the cosmic dance that destroys and recreates the universe, framed by a ring of fire and trampling the dwarf of ignorance. Chola bronzes like this were carried in temple processions, dressed in silk and jewels. They are among the masterpieces of world metal sculpture. Each bronze was cast in a single piece using the lost-wax method, so no two are exactly alike. Bronze-casters in Swamimalai in Tamil Nadu still work the same way today.

items.title: Qutb Minar, Delhi
items.medium: Red and buff sandstone and marble; about 72.5 m high
items.where: In situ, Delhi (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
items.label: Qutb-ud-din Aibak, founder of the Delhi Sultanate, began this victory tower beside the first mosque of Delhi; his successor Iltutmish added storeys, and Firuz Shah Tughlaq rebuilt the top in the 14th century. About 72.5 metres tall, it is carved with bands of Arabic inscriptions.
items.narration: Qutb Minar, Delhi. Qutb-ud-din Aibak, founder of the Delhi Sultanate, began this victory tower beside the first mosque of Delhi; his successor Iltutmish added storeys, and Firuz Shah Tughlaq rebuilt the top in the 14th century. About 72.5 metres tall, it is carved with bands of Arabic inscriptions. The Iron Pillar, which you can see as a replica in the Classical India gallery, stands in the same courtyard – an older monument reused by the builders of the mosque.

items.title: The stone chariot, Hampi
items.where: In situ, Vittala Temple, Hampi, Karnataka (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
items.label: In the courtyard of the Vittala Temple stands a shrine for Garuda carved in the shape of a temple chariot. Hampi was Vijayanagara, capital of one of the largest empires in Indian history, which foreign visitors described as one of the richest cities in the world.
items.narration: The stone chariot, Hampi. In the courtyard of the Vittala Temple stands a shrine for Garuda carved in the shape of a temple chariot. Hampi was Vijayanagara, capital of one of the largest empires in Indian history, which foreign visitors described as one of the richest cities in the world. Vijayanagara reached its height under Krishnadevaraya. In 1565 the city was defeated and sacked after the Battle of Talikota, and its ruins now spread across a landscape of giant boulders.

items.title: A page from the Akbarnama
items.medium: Opaque watercolour and gold on paper
items.label: The Akbarnama, 'Book of Akbar', is the official history of the third Mughal emperor, written by his minister Abul Fazl. Teams of court artists illustrated it with vivid scenes of battles, hunts and court life, blending Persian, Indian and European ideas into a new Mughal style.
items.narration: A page from the Akbarnama. The Akbarnama, 'Book of Akbar', is the official history of the third Mughal emperor, written by his minister Abul Fazl. Teams of court artists illustrated it with vivid scenes of battles, hunts and court life, blending Persian, Indian and European ideas into a new Mughal style. Akbar could not read, but he loved books. He held debates between scholars of many faiths and promoted a policy of sulh-i kul, 'peace with all'.

items.title: The Taj Mahal, Agra
items.medium: White Makrana marble inlaid with semi-precious stones
items.where: In situ, Agra (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
items.label: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built this tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. Thousands of craftsmen worked for over twenty years on the marble mausoleum, its gardens, mosque and guest house. Its inlaid stonework and perfect symmetry made it a symbol of India across the world.
items.narration: The Taj Mahal, Agra. The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built this tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. Thousands of craftsmen worked for over twenty years on the marble mausoleum, its gardens, mosque and guest house. Its inlaid stonework and perfect symmetry made it a symbol of India across the world. The flowers on its walls are not painted: they are made of carnelian, jasper, lapis and other stones cut and set into the marble, a technique called pietra dura.

items.title: Wine cup of Shah Jahan
items.label: Carved from a single piece of white jade, this cup is shaped like half a gourd, with a handle in the form of a wild goat's head and a lotus base. An inscription records that it was made for Shah Jahan in 1657. It shows the Mughal love of carving hard stones.
items.narration: Wine cup of Shah Jahan. Carved from a single piece of white jade, this cup is shaped like half a gourd, with a handle in the form of a wild goat's head and a lotus base. An inscription records that it was made for Shah Jahan in 1657. It shows the Mughal love of carving hard stones. Jade was believed to change colour or crack if it touched poison, which made it a favourite material for royal cups.

centre.title: A wheel of the Sun Temple, Konark (replica)
centre.medium: Replica of carved stone, about 3 m across
centre.label: King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty built the Sun Temple at Konark as a giant stone chariot for the sun god Surya, drawn by seven horses on 24 carved wheels. Each wheel is about three metres across, and the shadows of its spokes can be read like a sundial.
centre.narration: A wheel of the Sun Temple, Konark (replica). King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty built the Sun Temple at Konark as a giant stone chariot for the sun god Surya, drawn by seven horses on 24 carved wheels. Each wheel is about three metres across, and the shadows of its spokes can be read like a sundial. The Konark wheel has become one of the best-known symbols of Indian craftsmanship, and the Sun Temple appears on the back of India's ten-rupee note.

quiz.q: Where did Prithviraj Chauhan defeat Muhammad of Ghor in 1191?
quiz.why: Prithviraj won the first battle of Tarain in 1191 but lost there in 1192.

quiz.q: Which dynasty built the Brihadishvara temple at Thanjavur?
quiz.why: The Imperial Cholas built the Brihadishvara temple and sent naval expeditions overseas.

quiz.q: Who founded the Mamluk, or Slave, dynasty in 1206?
quiz.why: Qutbuddin Aibak founded the dynasty; Iltutmish later consolidated it.

quiz.q: Who is the only woman among the twelve Alvars?
quiz.why: Andal is the only woman among the Alvars; Karaikkal Ammaiyar was a Nayanar.

quiz.q: Whom did Babur defeat at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526?
quiz.why: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat, founding the Mughal empire.

quiz.q: Where was Shivaji crowned Chhatrapati in 1674?
quiz.why: Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674.

wings.title: Colonial India
wings.subtitle: From traders to rulers
wings.intro: In 1498 the Portuguese navigator Vasco da Gama reached Calicut. Within two centuries Portuguese, Dutch, French and British trading companies had set up posts along India's coasts. The British East India Company turned trade into conquest after the Battle of Plassey in 1757, and after the great uprising of 1857 the British Crown took direct control. The age also brought railways, reform movements and the first stirrings of Indian nationalism.

items.title: Vasco da Gama
items.where: Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga, Lisbon
items.label: The Portuguese navigator reached Calicut on the Malabar coast in May 1498, opening a sea route from Europe to India around Africa. Portugal soon set up forts and trading posts, and from 1510 ruled Goa, which remained Portuguese until 1961.
items.narration: Vasco da Gama. The Portuguese navigator reached Calicut on the Malabar coast in May 1498, opening a sea route from Europe to India around Africa. Portugal soon set up forts and trading posts, and from 1510 ruled Goa, which remained Portuguese until 1961. Europeans came for spices – pepper, cinnamon, cloves – and for Indian cotton textiles, which were prized all over the world.

items.title: Clive meeting Mir Jafar after the Battle of Plassey
items.medium: Oil on canvas, by Francis Hayman
items.label: At Plassey in Bengal, Robert Clive's East India Company army defeated the Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah, largely because the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar had been bribed to hold back his troops. Mir Jafar became Nawab, and the Company became the real power in Bengal.
items.narration: Clive meeting Mir Jafar after the Battle of Plassey. At Plassey in Bengal, Robert Clive's East India Company army defeated the Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah, largely because the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar had been bribed to hold back his troops. Mir Jafar became Nawab, and the Company became the real power in Bengal. In 1765, after the Battle of Buxar, the Mughal emperor granted the Company the right to collect the revenue of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa – the foundation of British rule in India.

items.title: Tipu's Tiger
items.medium: Painted wood with a mechanical organ
items.label: Made for Tipu Sultan, ruler of Mysore, this life-size wooden tiger mauls a European soldier. Turning a handle works an organ inside that makes the tiger growl and the man wail. Tipu fought four wars against the East India Company; after he died defending Srirangapatna in 1799, the tiger was taken to London.
items.narration: Tipu's Tiger. Made for Tipu Sultan, ruler of Mysore, this life-size wooden tiger mauls a European soldier. Turning a handle works an organ inside that makes the tiger growl and the man wail. Tipu fought four wars against the East India Company; after he died defending Srirangapatna in 1799, the tiger was taken to London. Tipu called himself the Tiger of Mysore. Tiger stripes decorated his throne, his weapons and the uniforms of his soldiers.

items.title: Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi
items.label: In 1857 Indian soldiers of the Company army rose in revolt at Meerut, and the uprising spread across northern India. The Rani of Jhansi became one of its most famous leaders; she died fighting near Gwalior in June 1858. After the revolt, the British Crown took over the government of India.
items.narration: Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi. In 1857 Indian soldiers of the Company army rose in revolt at Meerut, and the uprising spread across northern India. The Rani of Jhansi became one of its most famous leaders; she died fighting near Gwalior in June 1858. After the revolt, the British Crown took over the government of India. Other leaders of 1857 included the last Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar, Nana Sahib, Tantia Tope, Kunwar Singh and Begum Hazrat Mahal of Awadh.

items.title: Sikandar Bagh, Lucknow, photographed by Felice Beato
items.label: The photographer Felice Beato took this picture of the Sikandar Bagh in Lucknow a few months after British troops stormed it in November 1857, during the relief of the besieged Residency. It is one of the earliest photographs of the aftermath of war – a reminder of the violence of the uprising.
items.narration: Sikandar Bagh, Lucknow, photographed by Felice Beato. The photographer Felice Beato took this picture of the Sikandar Bagh in Lucknow a few months after British troops stormed it in November 1857, during the relief of the besieged Residency. It is one of the earliest photographs of the aftermath of war – a reminder of the violence of the uprising. Photography was only about twenty years old at the time. Long exposures meant that early photographers recorded ruins and landscapes rather than action.

items.title: Raja Ram Mohan Roy
items.label: Ram Mohan Roy, often called the father of the Indian Renaissance, founded the Brahmo Sabha in 1828 to promote a reformed faith. He campaigned against sati, the burning of widows, which was banned in Bengal in 1829, and argued for modern education and a free press. He died in Bristol in 1833.
items.narration: Raja Ram Mohan Roy. Ram Mohan Roy, often called the father of the Indian Renaissance, founded the Brahmo Sabha in 1828 to promote a reformed faith. He campaigned against sati, the burning of widows, which was banned in Bengal in 1829, and argued for modern education and a free press. He died in Bristol in 1833. Later reformers such as Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule, Swami Dayanand Saraswati and Syed Ahmad Khan carried this spirit of questioning and reform across India.

items.title: Victoria Terminus, Bombay
items.where: In situ, Mumbai (now Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, UNESCO World Heritage Site)
items.label: India's first passenger train ran from Bombay to Thane on 16 April 1853. By the 1880s railways linked ports with the interior, carrying cotton, grain and people. Bombay's Victoria Terminus, designed by F. W. Stevens, blends Victorian Gothic with Indian motifs.
items.narration: Victoria Terminus, Bombay. India's first passenger train ran from Bombay to Thane on 16 April 1853. By the 1880s railways linked ports with the interior, carrying cotton, grain and people. Bombay's Victoria Terminus, designed by F. W. Stevens, blends Victorian Gothic with Indian motifs. Railways helped British trade, but they also brought Indians from distant regions together, and later carried leaders and ideas of the national movement across the country.

centre.title: Bronze cannon of Mysore (replica)
centre.medium: Replica of a cast-bronze cannon on a wooden field carriage
centre.label: Haidar Ali and his son Tipu Sultan built a modern army with European-style artillery cast in their own foundries. Mysore's forces also used iron-cased war rockets that impressed their British opponents. Many of Tipu's bronze cannons, decorated with tiger-stripe patterns, were captured in 1799 and are displayed today in Britain and India.

Mysore's forces also used iron-cased war rockets that impressed their British opponents. Many of Tipu's bronze cannons, decorated with tiger-stripe patterns, were captured in 1799 and are displayed today in Britain and India. Captured Mysore rockets were studied in Britain and inspired the Congreve rockets later used in the Napoleonic Wars.

wings.title: Freedom and the Republic
wings.subtitle: The road to independence
wings.intro: In 1885 the Indian National Congress met for the first time in Bombay. Over the next six decades the struggle for freedom grew from petitions into mass movements led by Mahatma Gandhi, alongside revolutionaries, reformers and leaders from every region and community. Independence came on 15 August 1947, together with the painful partition of the subcontinent. On 26 January 1950 India became a sovereign democratic republic under its own Constitution.

items.title: The first Indian National Congress
items.label: Seventy-two delegates from across India met at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay for the first session of the Indian National Congress, presided over by W. C. Bonnerjee. Early leaders such as Dadabhai Naoroji argued that British rule was draining India's wealth, and asked for a greater Indian voice in government.
items.narration: The first Indian National Congress. Seventy-two delegates from across India met at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay for the first session of the Indian National Congress, presided over by W. C. Bonnerjee. Early leaders such as Dadabhai Naoroji argued that British rule was draining India's wealth, and asked for a greater Indian voice in government. Later leaders such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak demanded more: 'Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it.'

items.title: Mahatma Gandhi
items.label: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and transformed the freedom movement with satyagraha – non-violent resistance. He led the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920–22, the Salt March of 1930 and the Quit India Movement of 1942, and campaigned for Hindu–Muslim unity and against untouchability.
items.narration: Mahatma Gandhi. Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and transformed the freedom movement with satyagraha – non-violent resistance. He led the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920–22, the Salt March of 1930 and the Quit India Movement of 1942, and campaigned for Hindu–Muslim unity and against untouchability. Gandhi was assassinated in Delhi on 30 January 1948, less than six months after independence. His ideas inspired civil rights movements around the world.

items.title: The Salt March
items.label: Gandhi and 78 followers walked about 385 kilometres from Sabarmati Ashram to the sea at Dandi to make salt in defiance of the British salt tax. The march drew worldwide attention, civil disobedience spread across India, and tens of thousands of people were arrested.
items.narration: The Salt March. Gandhi and 78 followers walked about 385 kilometres from Sabarmati Ashram to the sea at Dandi to make salt in defiance of the British salt tax. The march drew worldwide attention, civil disobedience spread across India, and tens of thousands of people were arrested. Salt was a brilliant choice: everyone needed it, rich or poor, and making it from seawater was simple – so anyone could join the protest.

items.title: Bhagat Singh
items.label: Bhagat Singh was a young revolutionary of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association. In April 1929 he and Batukeshwar Dutt threw harmless bombs into the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi and courted arrest, using their trial to spread their ideas. He was hanged in Lahore in March 1931, aged 23.
items.narration: Bhagat Singh. Bhagat Singh was a young revolutionary of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association. In April 1929 he and Batukeshwar Dutt threw harmless bombs into the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi and courted arrest, using their trial to spread their ideas. He was hanged in Lahore in March 1931, aged 23. His slogan 'Inquilab Zindabad' – 'Long live the revolution' – became one of the most famous cries of the freedom struggle.

items.title: Subhas Chandra Bose
items.label: Twice elected president of the Congress, Subhas Chandra Bose broke with Gandhi over methods and escaped from British house arrest in 1941. In South-East Asia he led the Indian National Army, which fought alongside Japan in north-east India in 1944.
items.narration: Subhas Chandra Bose. Twice elected president of the Congress, Subhas Chandra Bose broke with Gandhi over methods and escaped from British house arrest in 1941. In South-East Asia he led the Indian National Army, which fought alongside Japan in north-east India in 1944. The trials of INA officers at Delhi's Red Fort in 1945 and 1946 caused a wave of protest across India, and convinced many British officials that their rule could not last.

items.title: Partition, August 1947
items.label: Independence came with the partition of British India into India and Pakistan. Around fifteen million people crossed the new borders in Punjab and Bengal, and the violence claimed hundreds of thousands of lives – some estimates say up to two million. It was one of the largest migrations in human history.
items.narration: Partition, August 1947. Independence came with the partition of British India into India and Pakistan. Around fifteen million people crossed the new borders in Punjab and Bengal, and the violence claimed hundreds of thousands of lives – some estimates say up to two million. It was one of the largest migrations in human history. Many families who lived through Partition have recorded their memories, so that the human cost of these events is not forgotten.

items.title: The Constitution of India
items.label: The Constituent Assembly, chaired by Rajendra Prasad, with B. R. Ambedkar leading the drafting committee, debated the Constitution for nearly three years. The original copies were hand-written by Prem Behari Narain Raizada and illuminated by artists of Santiniketan under Nandalal Bose. Its Preamble promises justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.
items.narration: The Constitution of India. The Constituent Assembly, chaired by Rajendra Prasad, with B. R. Ambedkar leading the drafting committee, debated the Constitution for nearly three years. The original copies were hand-written by Prem Behari Narain Raizada and illuminated by artists of Santiniketan under Nandalal Bose. Its Preamble promises justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. It is one of the longest written national constitutions in the world. Universal adult suffrage gave every citizen over twenty-one the vote, regardless of caste, religion, gender or wealth.

centre.title: A spinning wheel, or charkha (replica)
centre.medium: Replica in wood and cotton thread
centre.label: Gandhi urged every Indian to spin cotton every day. Spinning khadi – hand-spun, hand-woven cloth – was a way to boycott British mill cloth, give work to villagers and show self-reliance. In 1921 a spinning wheel was placed at the centre of a proposed national flag, the forerunner of the Ashoka Chakra on today's tricolour.
centre.narration: A spinning wheel, or charkha (replica). Gandhi urged every Indian to spin cotton every day. Spinning khadi – hand-spun, hand-woven cloth – was a way to boycott British mill cloth, give work to villagers and show self-reliance. In 1921 a spinning wheel was placed at the centre of a proposed national flag, the forerunner of the Ashoka Chakra on today's tricolour. Bonfires of foreign cloth were lit across India during the Non-Cooperation Movement, and wearing khadi became a badge of the freedom struggle.

wings.title: Themes of Indian History
wings.subtitle: Threads through time
wings.intro: History is more than kings and battles. This gallery follows long threads that run through India's past: centres of learning and science, art traditions, the meeting of many faiths, money and trade, and the work of historians who pieced the story together from inscriptions, coins, texts and archaeology.

items.title: Nalanda Mahavihara
items.where: In situ, Nalanda, Bihar (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
items.label: Founded under the Guptas in the 5th century, Nalanda grew into a great Buddhist monastic university with thousands of monks and teachers, drawing scholars such as Xuanzang from China. It flourished for some seven hundred years before its decline and destruction around 1200.
items.narration: Nalanda Mahavihara. Founded under the Guptas in the 5th century, Nalanda grew into a great Buddhist monastic university with thousands of monks and teachers, drawing scholars such as Xuanzang from China. It flourished for some seven hundred years before its decline and destruction around 1200. Students studied Buddhist philosophy, grammar, logic, medicine and astronomy. Its libraries were said to be so large that they burned for months when the monastery was destroyed.

items.title: Jantar Mantar, Jaipur
items.where: In situ, Jaipur (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
items.label: Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II built five astronomical observatories in north India. The one at Jaipur has 19 instruments, including the Samrat Yantra, a giant sundial that tells local time to an accuracy of about two seconds. It continued a long Indian tradition of astronomy going back to Aryabhata.
items.narration: Jantar Mantar, Jaipur. Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II built five astronomical observatories in north India. The one at Jaipur has 19 instruments, including the Samrat Yantra, a giant sundial that tells local time to an accuracy of about two seconds. It continued a long Indian tradition of astronomy going back to Aryabhata. Aryabhata, writing in 499 CE, explained that the Earth rotates on its axis, and calculated the value of pi to four decimal places.

items.title: Madhubani painting
items.label: For generations women in the Mithila region of Bihar painted the walls of their homes with gods, nature and wedding scenes in bold lines and bright colours. After a drought in the 1960s the art moved onto paper and became an important source of income.
items.narration: Madhubani painting. For generations women in the Mithila region of Bihar painted the walls of their homes with gods, nature and wedding scenes in bold lines and bright colours. After a drought in the 1960s the art moved onto paper and became an important source of income. India has hundreds of such living traditions – Warli in Maharashtra, Pattachitra in Odisha, Gond in Madhya Pradesh – each passed from one generation to the next.

items.title: Harmandir Sahib (the Golden Temple), Amritsar
items.label: The holiest gurdwara of Sikhism was built by Guru Arjan, who installed the Adi Granth here in 1604. Doors on all four sides welcome everyone, and its community kitchen feeds tens of thousands of people free every day. Maharaja Ranjit Singh covered its upper storeys in gilded copper.
items.narration: Harmandir Sahib (the Golden Temple), Amritsar. The holiest gurdwara of Sikhism was built by Guru Arjan, who installed the Adi Granth here in 1604. Doors on all four sides welcome everyone, and its community kitchen feeds tens of thousands of people free every day. Maharaja Ranjit Singh covered its upper storeys in gilded copper. India is the birthplace of Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism, and home for many centuries to Islam, Christianity, Judaism and Zoroastrianism.

items.title: The rupiya of Sher Shah Suri
items.label: Sher Shah Suri, who briefly drove the Mughal emperor Humayun out of India, introduced a standard silver coin called the rupiya. The Mughals and later the British kept it, and its name lives on in the rupee used in India and several neighbouring countries.
items.narration: The rupiya of Sher Shah Suri. Sher Shah Suri, who briefly drove the Mughal emperor Humayun out of India, introduced a standard silver coin called the rupiya. The Mughals and later the British kept it, and its name lives on in the rupee used in India and several neighbouring countries. Sher Shah also rebuilt the great road from Bengal to the north-west, later called the Grand Trunk Road, with rest houses and wells along the way.

items.title: Ashoka's inscriptions and the decipherment of Brahmi
items.label: For centuries no one could read the inscriptions on Ashoka's pillars and rocks. In 1837 James Prinsep, building on the work of many scholars, deciphered the Brahmi script, the ancestor of most South and South-East Asian scripts. A forgotten emperor spoke again.
items.narration: Ashoka's inscriptions and the decipherment of Brahmi. For centuries no one could read the inscriptions on Ashoka's pillars and rocks. In 1837 James Prinsep, building on the work of many scholars, deciphered the Brahmi script, the ancestor of most South and South-East Asian scripts. A forgotten emperor spoke again. Historians use many kinds of sources: inscriptions, coins, texts, travellers' accounts, art and the remains found by archaeologists. Each tells part of the story, and new finds can change it.

centre.title: Aryabhata, India's first satellite (replica)
centre.medium: Replica; the original was a 26-sided polyhedron about 1.4 m across, weighing 360 kg
centre.label: Named after the 5th-century mathematician and astronomer, India's first satellite was designed and built by ISRO in Bengaluru and launched by a Soviet rocket on 19 April 1975. Its faces were covered with solar cells. It carried experiments in X-ray astronomy and solar physics.
centre.narration: Aryabhata, India's first satellite (replica). Named after the 5th-century mathematician and astronomer, India's first satellite was designed and built by ISRO in Bengaluru and launched by a Soviet rocket on 19 April 1975. Its faces were covered with solar cells. It carried experiments in X-ray astronomy and solar physics. Aryabhata began a journey that led to India's own launch rockets, the Chandrayaan missions to the Moon and the Mangalyaan mission to Mars.
